This workflow uses the output data from Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing or Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing to calculate the bbb values for both the forward (anodic) and reverse (cathodic) scans by performing power-law fitting on the currents at the midpoint potential across different scan rates, enabling determination of the kinetic control mechanism of the electrode reaction.
data.fitting-method#Fitting Method: Least-squares linear fitting is performed in the log⁡ν\log \nulogν–log⁡i\log ilogi space to obtain the bbb values and goodness-of-fit R2R^2R2 for the anodic and cathodic processes, respectively.
data.midpoint-potential-selection#Midpoint Po:
This workflow uses the current values at the midpoint EmidE_{\text{mid}}Emid​ of the potential window as the analysis subject:
Emid=Ehigh+Elow2E_{\text{mid}} = \frac{E_{\text{high}} + E_{\text{low}}}{2}Emid​=2Ehigh​+Elow​​For the last complete cycle in each scan rate file, the absolute values of the current at EmidE_{\text{mid}}Emid​ during the forward scan and reverse scan are extracted separately, denoted as iai_aia​ (anodic current) and ici_cic​ (cathodic current).
data.output#Output: Log-log scatter plot with fitting lines: The x-axis is scan rate ν\nuν (V/s) and the y-axis is current iii (A), both in logarithmic scale. The plot includes anodic (red) and cathodic (blue) data sets with their fitting lines, and the legend annotates the bbb values and R2R^2R2. Data files: Raw data and fitting curve data are exported as separate CSV files.

The bbb value is used to determine the rate-controlling step of the electrode process:

data.determination-of-double-layer-capacitanc:
This workflow uses the output data from Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing or Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing to obtain the double-layer capacitance CdlC_{\text{dl}}Cdl​ through linear fitting of the difference between anodic and cathodic currents at the midpoint potential across different scan rates, which can be further used to calculate the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA).
Prerequisites You must first run Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing or Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing to complete CV data extraction. The input folder should contain CV extraction results at multiple different scan rates.
Procedure Select the input folder: Use the file picker to select the folder containing the CV data at different scan rates output by Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing or Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing. The system automatically calculates ΔI/2\Delta I / 2ΔI/2 values at each scan rate, performs linear fitting, and generates a fitting plot. Scientific Principles Determination of Double-Layer Capacitance CdlC_{\text{dl}}Cdl​ In the non-Faradaic potential region, only double-layer charging and discharging occurs at the electrode surface. Under these conditions, the charging current ici_cic​ is proportional to the scan rate ν\nuν:
ic=Cdl⋅νi_c = C_{\text{dl}} \cdot \nuic​=Cdl​⋅νIn practice, the average of the absolute values of the anodic current iai_aia​ and cathodic current ici_cic​ at the midpoint potential EmidE_{\text{mid}}Emid​ is taken as the approximate double-layer charging current at that scan rate:
ΔI2=∣ia−ic∣2\frac{\Delta I}{2} = \frac{|i_a - i_c|}{2}2ΔI​=2∣ia​−ic​∣​where EmidE_{\text{mid}}Emid​ is defined as:
Emid=Ehigh+Elow2E_{\text{mid}} = \frac{E_{\text{high}} + E_{\text{low}}}{2}Emid​=2Ehigh​+Elow​​
data.electrochemically-active-surface-area#El:
Given the specific capacitance CsC_sCs​ (unit: μF/cm2\mu\text{F/cm}^2μF/cm2) of a particular electrode material in a specific electrolyte, the ECSA can be calculated as:
ECSA=CdlCs\text{ECSA} = \frac{C_{\text{dl}}}{C_s}ECSA=Cs​Cdl​​A common reference value: the CsC_sCs​ of a smooth metal electrode surface is typically taken as 202020–60 μF/cm260\;\mu\text{F/cm}^260μF/cm2.
data.linear-fitting#Linear Fitting:
A linear fit is performed with ν\nuν on the x-axis and ΔI/2\Delta I / 2ΔI/2 on the y-axis:
ΔI2=Cdl⋅ν+b\frac{\Delta I}{2} = C_{\text{dl}} \cdot \nu + b2ΔI​=Cdl​⋅ν+bThe slope of the fit yields the double-layer capacitance CdlC_{\text{dl}}Cdl​ (unit: F). Ideally, the intercept bbb should approach zero.
data.output#Output: Linear fitting plot: The x-axis is scan rate ν\nuν (V/s), and the y-axis is ΔI/2\Delta I / 2ΔI/2 (A). The plot includes experimental data points (scatter) and the least-squares fitting line, annotated with the CdlC_{\text{dl}}Cdl​ value and R2R^2R2. Result files are saved to the output folder.

data: This workflow uses the output data from Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing to calculate the charge passed during the forward scan and reverse scan of each cycle via numerical integration, yielding coulombic efficiency and electrode capacitance.
data.capacitance-calculation#Capacitance Calc:
For electrode materials exhibiting capacitive behavior, the capacitance CCC is defined as the ratio of charge to the potential window ΔE\Delta EΔE:
C=QΔE=∫∣I∣ dtEhigh−ElowC = \frac{Q}{\Delta E} = \frac{\int |I|\, \mathrm{d}t}{E_{\text{high}} - E_{\text{low}}}C=ΔEQ​=Ehigh​−Elow​∫∣I∣dt​where EhighE_{\text{high}}Ehigh​ and ElowE_{\text{low}}Elow​ are the upper and lower limits of the scan potential window, respectively.
data.charge-calculation#Charge Calculation:
By definition of current, the charge QQQ is the integral of current III over time ttt. For discrete data, numerical integration is performed using the trapezoidal rule:
Q=∫t1t2I(t) dt≈∑k=1N−1I(tk)+I(tk+1)2⋅ΔtQ = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} I(t)\, \mathrm{d}t \approx \sum_{k=1}^{N-1} \frac{I(t_k) + I(t_{k+1})}{2} \cdot \Delta tQ=∫t1​t2​​I(t)dt≈k=1∑N−1​2I(tk​)+I(tk+1​)​⋅Δtwhere the time step Δt\Delta tΔt is derived from the sample interval and scan rate:
Δt=ΔEsampleν\Delta t = \frac{\Delta E_{\text{sample}}}{\nu}Δt=νΔEsample​​Here, ΔEsample\Delta E_{\text{sample}}ΔEsample​ is the sampling potential interval (V), and ν\nuν is the scan rate (V/s).
data.coulombic-efficiency#Coulombic Efficienc:
Coulombic efficiency (CE) is defined as the ratio of the charge passed during the reverse scan (reduction process) to the charge passed during the forward scan (oxidation process):
ηCE=QreverseQforward×100%\eta_{\text{CE}} = \frac{Q_{\text{reverse}}}{Q_{\text{forward}}} \times 100\%ηCE​=Qforward​Qreverse​​×100%This metric reflects the degree of reversibility of the electrode process. For an ideal, fully reversible process, the coulombic efficiency should approach 100%.
data.detailed_per_cycle#Detailed_Per_Cycle:
Detailed calculation results for each cycle in each file:
Field Description Q_Forward / Q_Reverse Forward/reverse scan charge (C) CE (%) Coulombic efficiency Cap_Forward / Cap_Reverse Forward/reverse scan capacitance (F) Cap_Avg Average capacitance (F)
data.output-files#Output Files: Upon completion, a Coulombic_Efficiency.xlsx file is generated containing the following two worksheets:
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites: You must first run Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing to complete CV data extraction and obtain Excel files, each containing the Scans_Split worksheet. Note: Output data from Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing is not currently supported.
data.procedure#Procedure: Select the input folder: Use the file picker to select the folder containing the Excel data files output by Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing. This folder typically contains CV extraction results at different scan rates. The system automatically completes the calculations and generates result files and visualization plots.
data.subsequent-analysis#Subsequent Analysis: Based on the output of this workflow, you can proceed with pseudocapacitance analysis such as CV/Pseudocapacitance Analysis: b-Value Kinetic Analysis or CV/Cdl: Double-Layer Capacitance and Electrochemically Active Surface Area Analysis.
data.summary_stats#Summary_Stats: Coulombic efficiency and capacitance statistics (mean and standard deviation) grouped by scan rate, used for evaluating the repeatability and stability of the test data.

data:
This workflow processes raw text-format (.txt) CV data exported from CHI (CH Instruments) electrochemical workstations. It automatically identifies test parameters, splits the continuous test curve into individual cycles, precisely aligns and pairs the data according to scan direction (forward/reverse), and exports the results as structured Excel spreadsheets.
This workflow serves as the data foundation for all subsequent CV analysis workflows.
data.cv-scan-segmentation-principle#CV Scan S:
Cyclic voltammetry characterizes electrochemical behavior by applying a triangular potential waveform to the working electrode. A complete cycle typically consists of two scan segments:
Forward Scan: The potential increases in the positive direction, corresponding to the anodic process. Reverse Scan: The potential decreases in the negative direction, corresponding to the cathodic process.
data.cycle-splitting#Cycle Splitting:
Scan direction changes are identified by detecting turning points in the potential sequence. A data point is identified as a turning point when the potential EiE_iEi​ satisfies the following condition:
Ei≈Ehigh or Ei≈Elow,(Ei−Ei−1)⋅(Ei+1−Ei)≤0E_i \approx E_{\text{high}} \;\text{or}\; E_i \approx E_{\text{low}}, \quad (E_i - E_{i-1}) \cdot (E_{i+1} - E_i) \leq 0Ei​≈Ehigh​orEi​≈Elow​,(Ei​−Ei−1​)⋅(Ei+1​−Ei​)≤0Endpoint Completion: Due to hardware sampling rate limitations, the last recorded data point may not have fully reached the set EhighE_{\text{high}}Ehigh​ or ElowE_{\text{low}}Elow​. The system automatically performs mathematical interpolation to ensure each scan segment lies within the strictly defined potential window [Elow, Ehigh][E_{\text{low}},\, E_{\text{high}}][Elow​,Ehigh​], thereby eliminating systematic errors in subsequent integration calculations caused by inconsistent windows.
data.data-alignment-and-closure#Data Alignmen:
To ensure curve continuity, the system implements cross-scan alignment:
Ensures that the endpoint of the preceding scan segment coincides with the starting point of the following scan segment in physical space. In Full Cycles mode, forces the data to start and close at the lowest potential, enabling direct use for plotting or integration calculations.
data.data-format#Data Format:
You should select a folder containing the raw data files for each scan rate. Each raw data file follows a format similar to:
Nov. 11, 2025 15:18:24 Cyclic Voltammetry File: d:\cv-1.bin Data Source: Experiment Instrument Model: CHI760F 4-electrode Header: Note: Init E (V) = 0 High E (V) = 0.4 Low E (V) = 0 Init P/N = P Scan Rate (V/s) = 1 Segment = 12 Sample Interval (V) = 0.001 Quiet Time (sec) = 2 Sensitivity (A/V) = 1e-4 Results: Channel 1: Segment 1: Segment 2: Segment 3: Segment 4: Segment 5: Segment 6: Segment 7: Segment 8: Segment 9: Segment 10: Segment 11: Segment 12: Potential/V, Current/A 0.000, -4.207e-6 0.001, -3.163e-6 0.002, -2.341e-6 0.003, -1.676e-6 0.004, -1.170e-6 0.005, -6.959e-7 0.006, -2.214e-7 0.007, 1.898e-7 0.008, 6.326e-7 0.009, 1.075e-6 0.010, 1.455e-6
data.faq#FAQ: Scientific notation: The system automatically recognizes current values in scientific notation formats such as 1.0e-03. Incomplete cycles: If a cycle is incomplete (containing only a unidirectional scan), the system retains and marks that segment without affecting the normal processing of the remaining cycles.
data.full_cycles#Full_Cycles: Data arranged by complete cycle, with each cycle containing a full forward scan and reverse scan. Used for plotting multi-cycle overlaid CV curves and observing cycling stability.
data.metadata#Metadata:
Records the original test conditions for the sample, including:
Parameter Description Unit init_e Initial potential V high_e / low_e Upper/lower limits of the potential window V scan_rate Scan rate V/s sample_interval Sample interval V
data.output-file-structure#Output File Struct: The output Excel files (one .xlsx file per original .txt file) contain three worksheets:
data.procedure#Procedure: Select the input folder: Use the file picker to select the folder containing the .txt raw data files exported from the electrochemical workstation. After automatic processing is complete, the output folder will be displayed in the interface and can be opened directly by clicking on it. An overlaid plot of the last-cycle CV curves at each scan rate is also generated automatically for a quick preview of data quality.
data.scans_split#Scans_Split: Forward scans and reverse scans are fully separated, formatted as C{n}_forward and C{n}_reverse. This worksheet is the core input data for subsequent analysis workflows such as CV: Coulombic Efficiency and Capacitance Calculation, CV/Pseudocapacitance Analysis: b-Value Kinetic Analysis, and CV/Cdl: Double-Layer Capacitance and Electrochemically Active Surface Area Analysis.

data: This workflow extracts the last complete cycle at each scan rate from multi-cycle CV data output by Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing or Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing, and overlays the steady-state CV curves from different scan rates on a single plot for intuitive comparison of electrochemical response characteristics across scan rates.
data.curve-concatenation-and-plotting#Curve C: For each scan rate, the potential–current data from the forward scan and reverse scan are concatenated end-to-end to form a complete, closed CV curve. Curves at different scan rates are distinguished by a colormap, and the legend automatically labels the corresponding scan rate (the display unit—V/s, mV/s, or μV/s—is selected automatically based on the numerical magnitude).
data.output#Output: Overlaid CV plot (potential versus current), with Potential (V) on the x-axis and Current (A) on the y-axis. The image is saved in PNG format to the input folder.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites: You must first run Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing or Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing to complete CV data extraction and obtain Excel files, each containing the Scans_Split worksheet.
data.principle#Principle: In cyclic voltammetry experiments, the electrode typically reaches an electrochemically stable state after multiple scan cycles. The CV curve from the last cycle is considered to best represent the intrinsic electrochemical behavior of the material at a given scan rate, and is therefore commonly used as the standard data for comparing responses across different scan rates.
data.procedure#Procedure: Select the input folder: Use the file picker to select the folder containing the Excel data files output by Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing or Cyclic Voltammetry (CV) Data Extraction and Preprocessing. The system automatically extracts the last complete cycle from each file and generates an overlaid CV plot.
data.selection-of-the-last-complete-cycle#Sel:
The system reads the Scans_Split worksheet and checks whether the last set of scan segments (the last 4 columns) contains complete forward and reverse scan data:
If the last cycle is complete (both forward and reverse scans contain data), it is used directly. If the last cycle is incomplete (containing only a unidirectional scan), the system falls back to the penultimate cycle.
data.subsequent-analysis#Subsequent Analysis:
Based on visual observation of the last-cycle data, you can proceed with the appropriate analysis path:
CV: Coulombic Efficiency and Capacitance Calculation: calculate coulombic efficiency at each scan rate CV/Pseudocapacitance Analysis: b-Value Kinetic Analysis: perform pseudocapacitive b-value kinetic analysis

data: EIS Extraction: CHI Instruments Data Preprocessing In-Situ EIS Extraction: DH Instruments EIS Plotting: Nyquist and Bode Visualization EIS/DRT Analysis: Mapping Frequency-Domain Impedance to a Distribution of Relaxation Times EIS/DRT Heatmap: Combining Multiple Samples’ Relaxation Time Distributions into a 2D View

If you have already reviewed the Nyquist and Bode plots but want to understand which kinetic process is dominating the response, this workflow is designed for exactly that purpose.
It performs DRT (Distribution of Relaxation Times) analysis on extracted EIS data, mapping frequency-domain impedance information onto a time-constant distribution. This makes it much easier to distinguish different processes visually (e.g., interfacial charge transfer, diffusion-related processes, etc.).
data.analysis-and-fitting-results#Analysis an:
Each sample produces the following data files:
fit_data.csv: experimental impedance, DRT-reconstructed impedance, and residuals drt_data.csv: τ\tauτ and γ(τ)\gamma(\tau)γ(τ) distribution summary.json: regularization parameters and solver summary (e.g., lambda_value, epsilon) Along with the following visualization plots:
nyquist_fit.png: experimental vs. DRT-fitted Nyquist comparison drt_tau.png: γ\gammaγ–τ\tauτ distribution plot (log-scale x-axis) residuals.png: real/imaginary residual plot *_drt_plots.opju: Origin project (containing Nyquist, DRT, and residual plots)
data.faq#FAQ: Why are there no results for some samples? The most common reason is missing input columns or invalid values in the data. The program skips these samples and reports the specific error.
data.practical-tips#Practical Tips: If this is your first time running DRT, it is a good idea to use EIS Plotting: Nyquist and Bode Visualization first to verify that the curves are smooth and free of obvious outliers. Doing so before entering this step typically yields more stable and more interpretable results.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites: Run EIS Extraction: CHI Instruments Data Preprocessing or In-Situ EIS Extraction: DH Instruments first and ensure the input consists of standardized EIS CSVs containing freq_hz, z_real_ohm, and z_imag_ohm.
data.principle-brief#Principle (Brief):
DRT represents impedance as a superposition of processes with different time constants. The core idea can be written as:
Z(ω)=R∞+∫γ(τ)1+jωτ dln⁡τZ(\omega)=R_\infty + \int \frac{\gamma(\tau)}{1+j\omega\tau} \, d\ln\tauZ(ω)=R∞​+∫1+jωτγ(τ)​dlnτWhere:
The peak positions of γ(τ)\gamma(\tau)γ(τ) reflect the characteristic time scales of different processes The peak area and height relate to the contribution strength of each process This approach makes it significantly easier to resolve overlapping mechanisms compared to interpreting Nyquist semicircles alone.
data.procedure#Procedure:
You have two options:
Select a directory (batch-process all .csv files in it) Or select a single .csv file (process one sample only) The program automatically creates a drt_output directory and outputs results for each sample separately.

/en/docs/eis/drt/.title: EIS/DRT Analysis: Mapping Frequency-Domain Impedance to a Distribution of Relaxation Times

data: After running DRT analysis on a set of in-situ EIS measurements (across different potentials or time points) or a series of samples (different conditions, different concentrations), overlaying all the γ(τ) curves on a single line plot quickly becomes unreadable. This workflow combines them into a single τ-versus-sample heatmap, using color to visually convey how the intensity of a given relaxation process evolves across conditions.
data.faq#FAQ: Why does it report “tau range no overlap”? If the frequency ranges of different samples do not overlap at all, the common τ grid cannot be constructed. Check the freq_hz column of the input data. How is the sample order determined? Natural sort: sample_001 < sample_002 < sample_010. If you do not want name-based ordering, rename the files beforehand. What if Origin custom Y ticks fail? The program catches the exception and falls back to numeric ticks. The .opju still opens correctly; only the Y-axis labels switch from sample names to 1, 2, 3, ....
data.output#Output: drt_heatmap.png: matplotlib heatmap, with τ on the x-axis (log scale) and the y-axis determined by the heuristic drt_heatmap.opju: Origin project — the primary deliverable for subsequent editing. The x-axis stores log₁₀τ values (the title reads log₁₀τ); this avoids the visual mismatch you would get if you laid linearly-spaced matrix cells under a log axis drt_heatmap_clipped.png / drt_heatmap_clipped.opju: clipped heatmap variant. DRT results often contain a single dominant peak that is much higher than every other feature, which stretches the color scale and washes out all secondary relaxation processes. These two files cap the color-scale upper bound at 120% of the second-tallest peak height (computed with scipy.signal.find_peaks on each sample’s γ(τ); the program takes the largest “second peak” across all samples, then multiplies by 1.2). Cells above the threshold are rendered with the top color of the scale. Both variants are produced alongside the originals so you can compare them side-by-side. If every sample has only one peak, the clipped variant is skipped and a console message is printed. drt_heatmap_matrix.csv: the interpolated γ matrix (not clipped), with the first column holding sample names, the second column the Y values, and the remaining columns headed by τ samples_meta.json: records y_mode, y_label, input_kind, and the sample-to-Y-value mapping In eis_csvs input mode, intermediate DRT results are also written to drt_heatmap/drt_output//drt_data.csv for reuse.
data.practical-tips#Practical Tips: For in-situ EIS data (sampled by time or potential), embed strictly increasing integer indices in the sample names (e.g., _001, _002). The y-axis will then automatically use those indices as coordinates, making it easy to align with other in-situ curves.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites:
Choose one of two input types:
A drt_output/ directory produced by [EIS/DRT Analysis: Mapping Frequency-Domain Impedance to a Distribution of Relaxation Times](/docs/eis/drt) (a collection of samples with DRT already computed) A directory of *_eis.csv files produced by [EIS Extraction: CHI Instruments Data Preprocessing](/docs/eis/extract_chi) or [In-Situ EIS Extraction: DH Instruments](/docs/eis/extract_in_situ_dh) (the program automatically runs DRT first, then plots) At least 2 samples are required.
data.principle-brief#Principle (Brief):
Each sample’s γ(τ) is interpolated onto a unified logarithmic τ grid, producing a matrix γi,j\gamma_{i,j}γi,j​, where iii indexes the sample (y dimension) and jjj indexes τ (x dimension). The heatmap encodes γi,j\gamma_{i,j}γi,j​ as color, making the following readable at a glance:
How the peak corresponding to a given relaxation process shifts along τ as conditions (potential/time) change Relative changes in peak intensity across samples
data.procedure#Procedure:
Select a single directory. The program automatically:
Detects the directory layout (drt_output/ versus *_eis.csv) Invokes the DRT solver if needed, caching each sample’s drt_data.csv to drt_heatmap/drt_output// Takes the intersection of all samples’ τ ranges, builds a 200-point logarithmic common grid, and linearly interpolates γ(τ) on the log-τ axis Naturally sorts the sample names Y-axis heuristic:
If every sample name ends with an integer that can be extracted, and those integers are all distinct (e.g., in_situ_001, in_situ_002, …), the Y-axis mode is index. Those integers become the Y values, and the axis is labeled Sample Index. Otherwise the workflow falls back to ordinal mode: Y values are 1..N, and the Y-axis ticks use the sample names (attempted in Origin via LabTalk; on failure, the axis falls back to numeric ticks with a console warning). The console prints the active mode for easy debugging.

data:
If you have just received raw .txt files exported from a CHI electrochemical workstation and are not sure where to begin, this workflow is the right starting point.
It automatically converts the raw EIS text into standardized tables (*_eis.csv) and fills in the key columns needed for subsequent plotting and fitting. You do not need to rename columns manually or worry about minor differences between export formats.
data.data-recognition-logic-brief#Data Recogn:
The program first locates the Freq/Hz header row, then automatically matches columns from common aliases:
Frequency column: Freq/Hz / Frequency/Hz / f/Hz Real-part column: Z'/ohm / Zreal/ohm / Z'/Ω Imaginary-part column: Z"/ohm / Z''/ohm / Zimag/ohm From these, it computes:
∣Z∣=Z′2+Z′′2,ϕ=arctan⁡(Z′′Z′)|Z| = \sqrt{Z'^2 + Z''^2}, \quad \phi = \arctan\left(\frac{Z''}{Z'}\right)∣Z∣=Z′2+Z′′2​,ϕ=arctan(Z′Z′′​)The phase angle is output in degrees (phase_deg).
data.output-file-description#Output File Desc:
Each *_eis.csv contains at least:
freq_hz: frequency (Hz) z_real_ohm: real part of impedance (Ω) z_imag_ohm: imaginary part of impedance (Ω) z_mod_ohm: impedance modulus (Ω) phase_deg: phase angle (°)
data.procedure#Procedure: Select the input folder: choose the directory containing the raw CHI .txt EIS files. The system traverses all .txt files in the directory and processes them one by one. On completion, an xxx-eis-extract output folder is created alongside the input directory. If a file has an unexpected format, the system skips it with a warning and continues processing the remaining files.
data.subsequent-analysis#Subsequent Analysis: EIS Plotting: Nyquist and Bode Visualization: quickly review Nyquist/Bode plot quality and trends EIS/DRT Analysis: Mapping Frequency-Domain Impedance to a Distribution of Relaxation Times: perform DRT (Distribution of Relaxation Times) analysis
data.what-you-get#What You Get: One *_eis.csv file per sample Unified fields: freq_hz, z_real_ohm, z_imag_ohm, z_mod_ohm, phase_deg Invalid data automatically removed (e.g., non-positive frequencies, empty values) Automatically sorted by frequency from high to low, ready for direct use in Nyquist/Bode/DRT workflows

data: This workflow processes in-situ EIS recordings that contain multiple Freq(Hz),Zre(Ω),Zim(Ω) blocks (e.g., 原位EIS数据参考.txt), automatically splitting them into individual standardized CSV segments. A new segment starts each time a new header row is encountered, making it well-suited for electrochemical degradation and trend analysis.
data.notes#Notes: Rows with frequency <= 0 or invalid numeric values are filtered out. If a segment contains no usable data, an error is reported for that segment and it is skipped. The output columns are fully compatible with EIS Extraction: CHI Instruments Data Preprocessing, so the files can be used directly with EIS Plotting: Nyquist and Bode Visualization and EIS/DRT Analysis: Mapping Frequency-Domain Impedance to a Distribution of Relaxation Times.
data.output-field-description#Output Field De: freq_hz: frequency (Hz, floating-point) z_real_ohm: real part (Ω) z_imag_ohm: imaginary part (Ω) z_mod_ohm: modulus ∣Z∣=Z′2+Z′′2|Z| = \sqrt{Z'^2 + Z''^2}∣Z∣=Z′2+Z′′2​ phase_deg: phase angle (°)
data.procedure#Procedure: Select a single .txt input file (single-file interaction). The text is read and split into data blocks at each detected header. Each block is converted to unified columns: freq_hz,z_real_ohm,z_imag_ohm,z_mod_ohm,phase_deg. The output directory is named _eis_csv, with files named _eis_001.csv, ....
data.required-data-format#Required Data Forma:
Example content:
Segment3(控制电位EIS) Freq(Hz),Zre(Ω),Zim(Ω) 1E5,2.58944E0,-1.55539E0 7.94328E4,2.71237E0,-1.8413E0 ... Segment6(控制电位EIS) Freq(Hz),Zre(Ω),Zim(Ω) 1E5,2.59732E0,-1.50046E0 7.94328E4,2.72004E0,-1.76758E0 ... Make sure each EIS segment in the input text contains the following three column headers:
Freq(Hz) Zre(Ω) Zim(Ω) Columns are comma-separated, and every subsequent row should consist of numeric values:
Freq(Hz),Zre(Ω),Zim(Ω) 1E5,2.58944E0,-1.55539E0 7.94328E4,2.71237E0,-1.8413E0 ... Segment* labels are optional; the parser does not depend on them. Whenever Freq(Hz),Zre(Ω),Zim(Ω) is encountered, it is treated as a new header.

data:
Once you have finished extracting EIS data, the natural first step is to plot the results and assess the data quality.
This workflow batch-plots all extracted *_eis.csv files as Nyquist and Bode diagrams, letting you quickly spot sample differences, outliers, and measurement stability. It also exports an Origin project file so you can refine and publish figures later.
data.1-nyquist-plot#1) Nyquist Plot: x-axis: Z′Z'Z′ y-axis: −Z′′-Z''−Z′′ Useful for observing charge-transfer impedance, diffusion behavior, and the overall shape before equivalent-circuit fitting
data.2-bode-plot#2) Bode Plot: Magnitude plot: ∣Z∣|Z|∣Z∣ vs. frequency (log scale) Phase plot: Phase vs. frequency (log scale) Convenient for comparing response mechanisms across different frequency ranges
data.output#Output:
Each sample produces:
*_nyquist_matplotlib.png *_bode_matplotlib.png *_eis_plots.opju (single-sample Origin project) In addition, a merged file is generated:
eis_plots_merged.opju (multi-sample merged Origin project)
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites: Run EIS Extraction: CHI Instruments Data Preprocessing or In-Situ EIS Extraction: DH Instruments first and make sure the directory already contains standardized *_eis.csv files.
data.procedure#Procedure: Select the input directory: choose the output directory from EIS Extraction: CHI Instruments Data Preprocessing. The system automatically detects all *_eis.csv files and batch-plots them. The output directory is the input directory itself; once processing is complete you can view images and project files directly.
data.subsequent-analysis#Subsequent Analysis: EIS/DRT Analysis: Mapping Frequency-Domain Impedance to a Distribution of Relaxation Times: perform DRT analysis on the same set of *_eis.csv files

data: How Oparic works: first “extract”, then “analyze / plot”.
data.a-full-run-through-cv-as-an-example#A fu: Step 1 · Extract Gallery → CV → “CV Extraction: CHI” (or whichever extraction card matches your instrument). In the folder picker, select the folder containing the raw .txt files (not a single file). You will get -cv-extract, containing normalized .xlsx files. Step 2 · Analyze / Plot Back to the gallery → pick a CV analysis or plotting card (for example, “Plot the Last Complete Cycle”). In the folder picker, select the -cv-extract output folder produced by Step 1. The figure is generated automatically. If Origin ≥ 2021 is ready, Oparic also creates worksheets, plots in Origin, and saves an .opju file to the output folder, where you can keep refining in Origin.
data.faq#FAQ: Origin did not launch? The status bar will explain why. Excel files and preview images should still be generated; if the issue persists, contact technical support. Will it overwrite my existing plots? Yes. If Origin already contains earlier plots, Oparic will overwrite them. Save your work before launching — a warning dialog will appear in this case. “No txt files were processed successfully”: make sure you selected a folder, and that the folder contains raw files in the matching instrument format (picking the wrong extraction card causes a format mismatch). Wrong folder selected in Step 2: analysis and plotting cards read the .xlsx / .csv files produced by extraction. Do not point them at the raw data folder — those formats cannot be parsed directly.
data.preparation#Preparation: Install and launch Oparic (Windows). Register and sign in. Origin (optional, but recommended): Windows only, requires Origin ≥ 2021. Once installed, the status bar will show Origin as ready. If Origin is missing or its version is too old, the cards still run — they just will not auto-generate Origin plots.
data.the-core-model-two-steps#The core model::
flowchart LR A["Raw instrument data(.txt files exported from the instrument, etc.)"] -->|input| B["Step 1: extraction cardchosen by instrument formate.g. CV Extraction: CHI"] B -->|output foldernormalized .xlsx| C["Step 2: analysis / plotting cardtakes the extraction output
folder/files as inpute.g. Plot the Last Complete Cycle"] C --> D["Origin / Excel / images"] Step 1 (extract): pick an “XX Extraction” card that matches your instrument (for example, “CV Extraction: CHI” or “CV Extraction: DIGISIM”). The input is the folder of raw files exported from the instrument; the output is normalized .xlsx files written to a sibling folder named like -cv-extract. Step 2 (analyze / plot): pick an analysis or plotting card (for example, “Coulombic Efficiency”, “Plot the Last Complete Cycle”, or “b-value Analysis”). Its input is the output folder produced by Step 1. Each card lists “Prerequisites” — which extraction card must run first — and “Related Analyses” — recommended follow-up cards you can click through to.
